rows.explanation: The instability value of 0.83 is correct as a measurement, but it doesn't point to a design problem here. BorrowBookUseCase is an application-layer orchestrator. Its outgoing dependencies (lines 1-10) all point inward to stable abstractions: domain entities, errors, repository interfaces, a domain service, a value object, and the application's own DTO and ports (Clock and IdGenerator, lines 9-10). Nothing imports infrastructure. Its collaborators come in through the constructor (lines 22-28), so they can be swapped at the composition root. Few modules depend on it, which is normal for a use case: it is the entry point a driver calls, not something other code builds on. The Stable Dependencies Principle expects concrete use cases like this to be highly unstable, because they depend on stable things and almost nothing depends on them. The real problem would be the reverse: domain or shared modules depending on this class. The body (lines 30-43) only coordinates domain behaviour (policy check, book.checkOut, Loan.open, saves). It doesn't absorb logic that would make it a widely depended-on hub. The high score comes from the measure itself, not from a flaw in this design.

rows.explanation: LoanController is an inbound HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer, which is the outermost ring. Its outgoing dependencies are what you would expect from an adapter: three application use cases (src/infrastructure/http/LoanController.ts lines 1-3) and two HTTP helpers in the same folder (lines 4-5). It gets these through constructor injection (lines 8-12). Each method does the same thin job: turn the request into use-case input, call the use case, and map the result or error to an HTTP response (lines 14-36). It contains no business logic. In a layered or clean architecture the outermost layer is supposed to be unstable, so a high instability value is expected here. Very little should depend on a controller, apart from the composition root or router. An instability of 0.83 for this file is normal for its position in the design, not a sign of fragility. The real stability concerns are domain and application code becoming unstable or depending outward, and this file does neither: every dependency points inward or to sibling infrastructure helpers.

rows.explanation: src/infrastructure/http/ErrorMapper.ts has behaviour worth testing, so the missing paired test file is a real gap and not a trivial-file artefact. Lines 4-10 hold a code-to-status table: three NOT_FOUND codes map to 404 and two validation codes map to 400. This mapping sets the HTTP contract clients see, and it can be tested in isolation because it is a pure function with no I/O. A paired test is cheap here and clearly what the rule is meant to require.

The comment on line 11 says this file is "a second composition root used by acceptance tests". A module like this has to sit at the outermost, most concrete edge, and no production code should depend on it. Instability is only a problem when stable modules depend on an unstable one, which would break the Stable Dependencies Principle. There is no sign of that here: the file is a test helper, and its dependencies all point inward or sideways within infrastructure. So instability=1 is a threshold artefact on sound code, not an architectural defect.

rows.explanation: FF-CV03 is meant to catch two things: classes that use a Repository-style name but aren't repositories, and repositories that aren't named as repositories. `CsvReportWriter` in src/infrastructure/http/CsvReportWriter.ts is neither. Its name contains no repository term (line 4). Its only method, `write`, is a pure transformation (lines 5-8): it maps an in-memory `readonly LoanDto[]` into CSV rows (line 6) and returns the joined string with a header (line 7). It doesn't store, load, query or delete anything, and it doesn't touch a database, file system or collection, so it doesn't act as a repository that should carry the suffix. The only import is an application DTO (line 1), and there's no persistence dependency. I ignored the doc comment on line 3 when judging; the decision comes from what the method body does. The class is a formatter, and calling it a "Writer" is accurate. The rule most likely matched on a broad pattern such as the word "Write" or "Writer", or a method named `write`, and treated it as a sign of persistence. That makes this a false positive of the rule's mechanism, not a naming violation.

rows.explanation: The rule wants domain files to be stable, and here that measurement points at a real design problem. The finding gives an instability of 0.5, so half of this file's coupling is outgoing. Three of its four imports are other domain modules (Loan, Member and DomainError, src/domain/services/LoanPolicy.ts lines 1-3), which is ordinary coupling inside the layer. The fourth, at line 4, imports `SystemClock` from `src/infrastructure/system/SystemClock`. That is a domain service reaching outward into the infrastructure layer, a part of the codebase that changes often. The import exists only so that `assertCanBorrowToday` (lines 7-9) can create a concrete clock with `new SystemClock().now()`. This makes the domain depend on a concrete infrastructure class it cannot control, raises its instability, and makes the convenience method hard to test without the real system time. The actual business rule, `assertCanBorrow` (lines 11-18), already takes `now: Date` as a parameter and needs nothing from infrastructure. So the dependency is unnecessary, and the rule fired on a genuine problem rather than a threshold edge case.
